title: Wiggle Subsequence
statement:
A sequence *wiggles* when the gaps between neighbouring elements switch sign at every step: up, then down, then up, and so on, or down, then up, then down. A gap of zero is never allowed, and the first gap may go either way. A sequence of one element wiggles, and so does a pair of two different elements.

Given an integer array `nums`, return the length of its longest wiggling subsequence. A subsequence keeps some of the elements (possibly all of them) in their original order and drops the rest.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every subsequence is exponential, and a DP over pairs of indices is O(n²). The faster view: look at the array as a line chart. Inside a run that keeps climbing, only its top matters, and inside a run that keeps falling, only its bottom matters, because the most extreme value leaves the most room for the next turn. So the answer is one plus the number of times the direction of the chart really changes, ignoring flat steps.

## Approach

1. Start `count` at 1 (the first element alone always wiggles) and `prevDiff` at 0, meaning no direction yet.
2. For each `i` from 1, compute `diff`, the step from `nums[i - 1]` to `nums[i]`.
3. The step is a new turn when it goes up after a fall (or at the start), or goes down after a climb (or at the start). A zero step is never a turn.
4. On a turn, add one to `count` and remember the new direction in `prevDiff`. Otherwise the current run just extends, and the newer, more extreme value silently replaces the old peak or valley.
5. Return `count`.

## Example 1, step by step

For `nums = [1, 7, 4, 9, 2, 5]` the steps are `6, -3, 5, -7, 3`. The first step `6` goes up while `prevDiff` is 0, so `count` becomes 2. Each later step has the opposite sign to `prevDiff`, so `count` grows to 3, 4, 5 and finally 6, the whole array.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over the array with constant work per step.
- Space: O(1): only a counter and the last direction are kept.

## Pitfalls

- Update `prevDiff` only on a turn. Overwriting it on every step would make a flat step (diff 0) look like a fresh start and count an extra turn.
- Use `<= 0` and `>= 0` so the very first non-zero step counts, even after leading equal values such as `[3, 3, 3, 2, 5]`.
- An array of equal values has answer 1, not 0 or 2.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | length of the longest wiggle subsequence of the prefix seen so far |
| `prevDiff` | sign of the last counted turn (0 before the first one) |
| `i` | index of the current element |
| `diff` | step from `nums[i - 1]` to `nums[i]` |
| `turnsUp`, `turnsDown` | whether this step reverses the direction upward or downward |

narration.2: The first element on its own is always a wiggle sequence of length 1.
narration.3: No direction has been taken yet, so the last difference starts as 0.
narration.5: Walk through every neighbouring pair of elements.
narration.6: Measure the step from the previous element to this one.
narration.7: A rising step is a turn if the chart was falling or had no direction yet.
narration.8: A falling step is a turn if the chart was rising or had no direction yet.
narration.9: Only a real change of direction lengthens the subsequence; flat steps and continuing runs do not.
narration.10: Count the new peak or valley.
narration.11: Remember the new direction so the next turn must go the other way.
narration.14: Return the number of elements in the longest wiggle subsequence.
